questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I've always been fascinated by the US in general and by the idea of studying in the US, so that was always my top priority in choosing destination. More specifically, I chose CU Boulder because it's in a great location right next to the mountains providing many opportunities to hike, climb, ski etc. Furthermore, I was very drawn to Boulder, since it's a university town, so a lot of the town is centred around the university. I also read a lot of student reports on Boulder that were very positive.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was extremely easy. There was an international student orientation the week I got there, where I received all of the important information and picked up my ID-cards.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above, I simply showed up to the orientation, where I received all of the necessary information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was fairly difficult to find off campus housing. I scoured multiple Facebook groups for months and applied to all of the relevant postings. There is a certain element of luck involved. Bear in mind that most people don't love the fact that you're only there for one semester, so be sure to mention that as the first thing. I ultimately found housing through the "University of Colorado Boulder (UCB) Housing, Sublets and Roommates" Facebook group, so I would start there. It also goes without saying that you should start looking early, as everyone gets quite desperate for housing towards the end (including myself)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would 100% recommend living off campus. Living on campus is more expensive and you will end up living with students that are far younger (all freshmen) that probably have very different lifestyles. Furthermore, I would recommend trying to find something privately on Facebook or other groups. You can get off campus housing through the university through a company called Four Star Realty, but they are notoriously difficult to deal with, and you will likely end up living with other international students. This is, however, a safer option.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The biggest reason my semester abroad was rated a 10/10 was because of my roommates. I lived in a house with 8 other Americans (and 2 dogs) and truly immersed myself in the American culture and had an authentic "American experience". For this reason, I would absolutely recommend finding a place with other Americans. I lived on the Hill, which is where a lot of the people living off campus live. This is a great place to live in my opinion, since it's close to campus and to the mountains, so you get the best of both worlds.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Registering for courses was fairly easy. I simply found courses at the appropriate level that all sounded interesting and then got my academic advisor to sign up for them by sending them an email, since you can't do it yourself as an exchange student. After picking courses, I just got them approved through KU, and then there were no other issues.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You have an academic advisor who is very helpful, who can guide you through the whole thing and help you sign up for classes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all of the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: When picking courses I looked at two things: how interesting the course sounded, and how the teacher was rated. Don't think too much about the teacher's rating, if the class sounds interesting to you, but it can also make the class a lot less enjoyable, if you have a bad professor. My experience with professors were mostly good though.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took three 4000-level classes, which is officially equivalent to the third year at KU, but they were much easier. I also took one 3000-level class, which was probably my most difficult class, since it was very different to what I do normally and was a class from a different faculty.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: On the whole, it was a lot easier. Unlike at KU, where I had both lectures and classes with two different teachers, in Boulder I had just one professor doing both lectures and classes at the same time. It felt a lot more like high school than university in my opinion. For the most part, the classes were in the style of lectures, but were very discussion based, so it didn't necessarily feel like a lecture.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Natural Resource Economics
- Economics of Entrepreneurship
- International Political Economy
- Economic Growth

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I learned most from Natural Resource Economics and from International Political Economy. In Natural Resource Economics, the professor was incredibly engaged and interesting, and I learned a lot about natural resources in general and how they work in the US. International Political Economy was also a very interesting class and very different to what I normally do at KU. It was essay-based and every week we read articles about different political economy-oriented issues and then discussed them in class. It challenged me in a good way.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went on a few trips that ended up being fairly expensive, but it was definitely worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I was shocked by how expensive housing is in Boulder. I payed $1000 a month, which is even in the low end of how much you could end up spending. Food is also very expensive compared to Denmark, both food from the supermarket and when you eat out.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Anything you can think of. They seemingly have clubs for anything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was part of the Alpine Club and went on a few trips with them, which I highly recommend if you're into climbing. I also frequently went to the climbing gym at the rec center, where I met some really great people too.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are many beautiful places to visit both in and around Colorado. Go up to the Rocky Mountains National Park if you're into hiking and beautiful views. I also went on a trip to Yellowstone National Park, which was amazing, but you need to have access to a car to get there. Through the Alpine Club I went to Utah to go climbing over the weekend, which was a lot of fun too. Lastly, for Thanksgiving break, I went with some of my roommates to Chicago. Basically, it's a lot easier to go to different places in the US once you're already there, so either try to tag along on a trip or arrange your own. There are an endless amount of opportunities. I would also recommend going clubbing or to concerts in Denver if you're into that kind of thing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was extremely easy, since my roommates were so incredibly welcoming. They immediately made it feel like home.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs and engage in them. I didn't make too many friends from my classes, since I didn't spend that much time in classes, so seek out people with similar interests and I'm sure you will have no problem socialising. It's also a lot easier if you live with Americans that all have friends already you can meet.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Everything seemed very overwhelming at first, because it's such a big country and just going grocery shopping for the first time was a very intimidating experience, since there a million options for every single food item and the places are so huge. I also had to get used to how open and talkative Americans are, but I also love them for that.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Americans are all (mostly) really nice, generous and welcoming, and I felt extremely welcome as a non-American living in their country. I also love the culture that is unique to Boulder with how active and healthy everyone is, since I'm like that too.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Live with Americans if you can.
2. Don't worry about school. It will be a lot easier, and you should spend most of your time experiencing life in Boulder, because it is unlike Denmark in almost every way.
3. Join clubs or try to engage in campus life in some other way. There are so many opportunities. You just have to grab them.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: One thing I forgot to mention is that you can switch classes during the first couple of weeks, if you don't find one or more of the classes interesting. I switched one of my classes, and it was definitely worth it.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Gaining so many American friends and having had so many unique experiences that I wouldn't otherwise have had.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Leaving. Being away for one semester is strange, because I very quickly felt at home and fell in love with being there, and then all of a sudden it's over. All I can say is: Try to enjoy every day you have there, because even if each day isn't perfect in and of itself, you will look back on your time there fondly.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
